title: Trump administration weighs options to curb record US diesel costs - Bloomberg
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
Investing.com -- The Trump administration is actively evaluating a broad slate of emergency policy measures designed to stem soaring domestic diesel prices, ranging from federal tax suspensions to the temporary integration of untaxed off-road fuel supplies. Deliberations remain fluid with no immediate policy action deemed imminent, according to reporting from Bloomberg, as White House officials attempt to balance severe domestic margin pressures against growing trade and foreign policy complications.
The policy push follows unprecedented market turbulence after President Donald Trump voiced support for restricting foreign fuel shipments, driving sharp volatility across global energy futures. The prospect of an export ban has drawn fierce resistance from industry trade groups and sparked deep alarm among European allies, who remain heavily reliant on U.S. distillates amid ongoing geopolitical conflicts involving Iran and Russia.
With national retail diesel prices hovering near historic highs around $6.50 per gallon, oil executives are lobbying Washington to favor a temporary suspension of the federal excise tax over trade restrictions. However, a federal tax suspension faces immediate administrative headwinds, notably because the House of Representatives is currently in a pre-election recess, while efforts to alter biofuel-blending mandates have stalled due to agricultural state politics ahead of the November midterms.
In response to immediate supply strains during the critical autumn harvest, state leaders are taking localized action to bypass federal bottlenecks. Governors in key agricultural states, including Louisiana, Alabama, and Nebraska, have issued emergency declarations permitting commercial haulers to burn untaxed, red-dyed off-road diesel on public highways without regulatory penalty, offering temporary operational relief to midstream supply chains even as broader market tightness persists.

title: Trump seeks to withhold $800 million in Congress-approved funds
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
WASHINGTON, Sept 25 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump sought on Friday to unilaterally withhold more than $800 million in spending on immigration, race and education that Congress has approved.
The move was the latest salvo in a fight between the Trump administration and Congress over control of the nation’s spending.
"President Trump is committed to utilizing all possible tools to cut wasteful and harmful government spending that does not benefit American citizens," the White House said in a statement announcing the steps.
The statement outlined several programs, including some focused on refugee assistance, racial-minority business development and overseas conservation.
The Constitution gives Congress the power of the purse, but the White House said the programs supported illegal immigration, stoked racial tensions and promoted alarmist approaches to the environment.
The White House is deploying a rarely used technique known as a "pocket rescission" that bypasses Congress.
Senator Susan Collins, who chairs the chamber’s Appropriations Committee, described the step as "illegal."
"This is the most recent attempt by this Office of Management and Budget to undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse," said Collins, a member of Trump’s Republican Party fighting a tight race for reelection in Maine. "Any effort to rescind appropriated funds without congressional approval is a clear violation of the law."
The Supreme Court last year declined to block Trump from using the same tactic to withhold $4.9 billion in foreign aid Congress had approved, while litigation continued.

title: TikTok settles Alabama teen harm case for at least $100 million
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
Investing.com -- TikTok and parent ByteDance have agreed to pay Alabama at least $100 million to settle allegations that the video platform was designed to addict children and misled consumers about its safety, Reuters reported Friday.
The agreement marks TikTok’s first settlement with a U.S. state over claims concerning harm to young users and comes before Alabama’s case was set to become the first of the state lawsuits against the company to reach trial.
Alabama will receive at least $100 million within 45 days under the agreement, according to the state Attorney General’s office. The payment could rise to as much as $300 million if certain conditions are met.
The settlement removes the immediate prospect of a trial over allegations that TikTok and ByteDance made the platform addictive to younger users and misrepresented its safety.
Alabama’s case is part of a broader legal challenge facing TikTok across the U.S. At least 27 other states and Washington, D.C., have brought similar lawsuits against the company over its treatment of younger users.
TikTok has disputed such claims, arguing that teen safety has been a priority in designing its platform. The company has also cited Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which provides online platforms with certain protections from liability involving user-generated content.
The Alabama agreement follows a separate settlement between TikTok, ByteDance and the U.S. Justice Department over children’s privacy allegations. That deal calls for an immediate $300 million payment and another $100 million if a court ends a 2019 Federal Trade Commission consent decree involving TikTok predecessor Musical.ly.
A federal judge recently signalled that he may reject the request to terminate that decree, which requires TikTok to maintain certain reporting and record-keeping obligations through 2029.
The Alabama settlement leaves TikTok facing similar state-level litigation elsewhere in the U.S.

title: ShinyHunters hackers expanded attacks on Oracle’s PeopleSoft, Google says
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
Sept 25 (Reuters) - Google’s cybersecurity unit said on Friday that hacking group ShinyHunters has renewed "mass exploitation" of a security flaw in Oracle’s PeopleSoft software, after skirting defenses put up following attacks in the summer.
Mandiant made the announcement in a threat intelligence report released days after ShinyHunters, which has claimed responsibility for several major data breaches, said it had stolen FBI personnel data.
The evolving nature of the attack is likely to ring alarm bells at organizations that rely on PeopleSoft for human resources and other critical functions, and heighten concerns about the vulnerability of even well-resourced institutions.
The unit of Alphabet’s Google said ShinyHunters exploited a bug in Oracle’s PeopleSoft enterprise software in attacks from May 27 through June 9 that mainly affected universities.
Mandiant said the hackers adapted to defensive guidance published after the May-June attacks and targeted organizations that implemented web application firewall rules but did not apply an update that Oracle issued to patch the vulnerability.
It said, without identifying victims, that the latest attack affected dozens of systems globally in sectors as varied as higher education, technology, healthcare, agriculture, transportation and government.
ShinyHunters has said it accessed FBI data using a vulnerability in PeopleSoft. Reuters has not been able to corroborate the claim. Oracle did not respond to requests for comment.
In a statement issued Wednesday, the Federal Bureau of Investigation said it was "aggressively investigating" the reported breach.
ShinyHunters exposed the names of personnel working in sensitive FBI units and acquired medical and psychiatric records, Reuters previously reported.

title: TikTok reaches first state settlement over teen safety claims, agrees to user limits
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
(Corrects bullet-point formatting, no change to story text)
By Diana Novak Jones
Sept 25 (Reuters) - Alabama said on Friday it had reached a settlement with TikTok and its Chinese parent company, ByteDance, that requires the social media platform to impose new usage limits and enhanced age-verification measures for users in the state, resolving claims that the platform endangered children and misled consumers about its safety.
The agreement, which came days before a scheduled trial, calls for TikTok to implement changes for teenagers in Alabama including a two-hour daily time limit, pauses after 15 minutes of use and stricter age checks.
TikTok will pay Alabama at least $100 million under the settlement, but the state’s payout could grow to $300 million if 40 other attorneys general sign on to similar agreements with the company within a specified timeframe, according to the settlement.
"This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens," a spokesperson for TikTok’s US operations said in a statement.
The deal marks TikTok’s first settlement with a state in the sweeping litigation over social media’s impact on teen well-being. Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall sued the company last year, and at least 27 other states and Washington, D.C., have brought similar lawsuits.
"This is a great day for Alabama parents," Marshall said in announcing the agreement.
The trial, which had been scheduled to kick off Monday in Montgomery state court and expected to last two to three weeks, had been expected to provide a rare look inside TikTok, which has settled prior cases selected for trial and sought to keep details of its operations from public view.
Alabama had claimed TikTok’s endless stream of videos makes it the most addictive social media platform and that its algorithm pushes young users toward increasingly intense content about violence and self-harm, contributing to a teen mental health crisis and causing the number of emergency room visits for self-harm in the state to "skyrocket."
The lawsuit accused TikTok of falsely claiming it limits access to sexual and violent content for young users in order to have its app rated safe for teens in app stores run by Google, Apple and Microsoft and of misleading users about the Chinese government’s access to US users’ data.
TikTok has said it designed its platform with teen safety as a key priority and argued that Section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act shields online platforms from liability over user-generated content.
REDACTED DOCUMENTS, SEALED FILINGS
In addition to the states’ cases, TikTok faces thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts and municipalities over its alleged impact on young users’ mental health. Meta Platforms, Snap Inc and Alphabet’s YouTube are also defendants in many of these cases.
With the settlement in Alabama, TikTok has settled all cases selected for trial against it, including claims by five young people and a Kentucky school district.
Alabama’s lawsuit claimed TikTok asks users to self-report their ages, but it also allows users to evade its questions about their age by viewing videos without creating an account, which still allows the company to collect data on their viewing habits. The lack of an effective age restriction makes things like “Kids Mode,” which curates content for young users, entirely useless, according to the lawsuit.
The state also claimed the platform traps kids in so-called “filter bubbles,” feeding them increasingly intense content on subjects that capture their attention, including violent or harmful material.
Last month, Meta reached a sweeping $17.1 billion settlement with 47 states, Washington, D.C., and US territories. Meta, which did not admit wrongdoing, agreed to make changes to teens’ access to Instagram and Facebook as part of the deal and conditioned $5 billion of the payout on TikTok, Snap and YouTube’s adoption of those terms. TikTok has not said anything publicly about the deal.
Like the Meta settlement, Alabama’s deal with TikTok would require the company to adopt additional restrictions if its rivals Snap, Google and Meta make similar changes.
Those measures could further limit teens’ time on social media apps and restrict overnight access, according to the filing.
Although the settlement applies only in Alabama, major platform changes could prove difficult to implement on a state-by-state basis.

title: Iran awaits US response to Hormuz peace plan as Trump reportedly rejects deal
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
Investing.com -- Iran was awaiting an official U.S. response Saturday to a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and halt fighting across the Middle East, after the Wall Street Journal reported President Donald Trump had rejected the offer.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said the proposal, transmitted through Qatari mediators, would start a seven-day countdown to reopening the critical waterway and pausing regional hostilities.
Araqchi said an agreement could lead to broader negotiations between Washington and Tehran. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Iran would not compromise on its nuclear rights, including uranium enrichment or shipping highly enriched uranium abroad.
Iran’s proposal calls for hostilities to stop across the region, including in Lebanon. Washington would be required to lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian funds and waive oil sanctions.
A U.S. official previously described talks through mediators as "positive and constructive." The Journal reported Trump was privately sceptical Iran would meet U.S. demands and viewed renewed bombing as likely. Reuters said it could not independently confirm the report.
The diplomatic push comes seven months after U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran began the current conflict. Fighting has disrupted oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz, a major global energy route, and spread across the region.
Araqchi also briefed Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan on an understanding between Iran and Oman covering safe shipping routes through Hormuz.
Tensions around Saudi Arabia remain elevated. A Saudi-led coalition said Saturday it intercepted two Houthi drones headed toward Riyadh and a ballistic missile targeting Khamis Mushait.
The Houthis have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July. Their attacks have added pressure to oil transportation as traffic through Hormuz remains largely blocked.
Saudi Arabia has also strengthened regional defence coordination. Turkish and Pakistani defence officials met in Riyadh Friday to discuss intelligence sharing, military coordination and integration of forces, following talks between the three countries’ foreign ministers.
Markets have been sensitive to prospects for reopening Hormuz. Earlier reports of Iran’s proposal helped push Brent crude below $100 a barrel this week as traders assessed the possibility of improved Middle Eastern supply flows.

title: Bitcoin holds near $84,000 as rising bond yields offset regulatory progress
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
Investing.com -- Bitcoin steadied around $84,000 heading into the weekend, with rising U.S. Treasury yields pressuring the cryptocurrency even as institutional demand and regulatory developments offered support.
Bitcoin was trading at $83,981.2 as of 00:55 ET (04:55 GMT), down about 0.27% for the day. The cryptocurrency had briefly approached $85,000 Friday after dropping below $83,000 earlier in the week.
The main pressure came from the bond market. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield climbed above 5.2% Friday after reaching its highest level since 2007, raising the relative appeal of interest-bearing assets and weighing on Bitcoin and other risk assets.
Institutional flows provided a counterweight. U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds attracted about $2.65 billion across five consecutive sessions through Wednesday, including roughly $347 million on Wednesday. BlackRock’s IBIT and Fidelity’s FBTC accounted for most of that day’s inflows.
Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR), the largest corporate Bitcoin holder, is also seeking to expand its Bitcoin-linked financing model. The company proposed daily dividend accruals for four preferred stocks, arguing that more frequent payments could improve liquidity and demand for the securities. Stronger preferred-share demand could give Strategy greater access to capital for additional Bitcoin purchases.
Regulatory developments presented a mixed picture. SEC Commissioner Hester Peirce, a longstanding supporter of clearer cryptocurrency rules, will leave the agency Oct. 2 after helping lead its Crypto Task Force and recent work covering staking, token classification and tokenized securities.
Her departure follows another setback in Washington after the Senate failed to advance the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act. Blockchain Association CEO Summer Mersinger is also stepping down, with former leader Kristin Smith returning as interim CEO.
Outside the U.S., Germany’s proposed cryptocurrency tax reforms raised fresh concerns. A planned substitute assessment could calculate taxes using 50% of crypto sale proceeds when investors cannot provide credible acquisition-cost records, drawing criticism from Circle executive Patrick Hansen.
For Bitcoin, the weekend setup leaves strong institutional inflows and continued corporate adoption competing with elevated bond yields and lingering regulatory uncertainty.

title: Korea’s trade surplus hits a record $23B. Here’s what’s driving it
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
Investing.com -- South Korea’s trade surplus widened to a record $23 billion in the first 20 days of September as exports accelerated, led by strong semiconductor shipments and a sharp rebound in autos and auto parts, according to Goldman Sachs.
Exports per working day rose 7.4% month-on-month on a seasonally adjusted basis, accelerating from 4.1% in the previous month. Total exports during the first 20 days climbed 14.9%, compared with a 7.2% increase previously.
Some of the acceleration reflected front-loading ahead of the lunar Mid-Autumn Festival holidays in late September.
Semiconductors were the biggest contributor, with chip exports increasing 16% and accounting for roughly 60% of the sequential rise in overall exports.
Other technology exports fell 1%, though the pace of decline moderated from the previous month. Higher handset and household appliance shipments were offset by weaker computer exports.
Outside technology, autos and auto parts provided another major boost. Exports jumped 60.8% after contracting for two consecutive months and accounted for roughly a quarter of the overall sequential increase. Ship exports also rebounded sharply.
Demand from the U.S. was particularly strong, with exports to the country surging 48.1%, accelerating from 13.6% previously. The U.S. accounted for slightly more than half of the overall sequential export gain.
Shipments to Taiwan and the European Union climbed 43.6% and 34.7%, respectively, together contributing about 30% of the increase. Exports to mainland China grew by a more modest 1.2%.
Imports also strengthened across major categories including energy products, semiconductors and machinery. Total imports during the 20-day period increased 10.5%, compared with 1.7% previously.
The stronger export performance pushed the non-seasonally adjusted trade surplus to a historic $23 billion, up sharply from $14 billion in the previous month.

title: Larry Ellison adds $9.2 billion in Oracle shares as loan collateral
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
Investing.com -- Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) co-founder Larry Ellison has pledged an additional 67 million shares of the software company as collateral for personal loans compared with a year earlier, representing about $9.2 billion at Friday’s closing price, Bloomberg reported.
The additional shares represent a 19% increase in the amount of Oracle stock Ellison has pledged since 2025, according to a proxy filing released Friday.
Oracle shares closed Friday at $137.10. The total amount pledged as collateral now represents about 36% of Ellison’s holdings in the company. The 82-year-old technology billionaire owns about 1.16 billion Oracle shares.
The disclosure comes as Ellison helps finance his son David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance (NASDAQ:PSKY) in its planned $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery (NASDAQ:WBD).
The Ellisons have committed $47 billion in equity financing toward the Warner Bros. transaction, with about $24 billion coming from three Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds. Paramount is also seeking debt financing for the acquisition.
The Warner Bros. deal has moved closer to completion after Paramount negotiated a settlement earlier this week with 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild, which had sued to block the merger.
Oracle’s corporate policy prohibits officers and directors from pledging company shares as collateral for personal loans, with an exception for Ellison, who serves as executive chair and chief technology officer.
Earlier this month, Ellison disclosed plans to sell as much as $7.5 billion of Oracle stock before quickly cancelling the planned sale.

title: China agrees to buy 10 million tons of U.S. coal in 2027 and 2028
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
Investing.com -- China has agreed to purchase at least 10 million metric tons of U.S. coal in both 2027 and 2028 as Washington and Beijing expand trade cooperation following their latest high-level talks, Bloomberg reported.
The coal commitment forms part of agreements reached under the newly operational U.S.-China Board of Trade, according to a White House statement.
The two countries will also pursue preferential tariffs covering $30 billion of non-sensitive goods from both sides, potentially lowering trade barriers across a range of consumer and industrial products.
U.S. goods eligible for preferential tariff treatment include agricultural products, seafood, timber, cosmetics and medical devices. Chinese products covered by the agreement include small appliances, toys, holiday decorations and children’s car seats.
Agriculture will receive separate attention through a newly created working group tasked with addressing market-access barriers. The sector has repeatedly featured in trade negotiations between the two countries.
Washington and Beijing also established a Board of Investment to discuss investment opportunities and address obstacles facing companies seeking to invest across the two markets.
Critical minerals remain another area of negotiation. The countries agreed to continue discussions over U.S. concerns about supply-chain shortages involving rare earths and other critical minerals, which are used across technology, automotive and defence industries.
President Donald Trump also urged Chinese President Xi Jinping to increase China’s production of refined petroleum products as the U.S. seeks to stabilise global supplies amid disruptions linked to the Middle East conflict.
Technology will form another part of the bilateral discussions. Washington and Beijing agreed to continue talks covering emerging technologies, with their next exchange focused on artificial intelligence scheduled to take place by November.
The agreements follow the three-day Trump-Xi summit in Washington, where trade, technology, critical minerals and other economic issues featured prominently.
The coal purchase commitment provides a concrete trade measure from the talks, with China set to import at least 20 million metric tons of U.S. coal across the two years.

title: BofA explains how telecom companies can evolve to be AI winners
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
Investing.com -- European telecom operators could benefit from adopting artificial intelligence across sales and customer retention, even as AI agents help consumers find cheaper deals, Bank of America analysts said.
Reports are emerging of AI agents researching telecom packages and contacting providers to negotiate better terms for customers. Such tools could increase pressure on operators by making price comparisons and switching easier.
Yet price arbitrage has shaped European telecom markets for about 15 years, driven by entrants such as Iliad and the growth of mobile virtual network operators. Consumers are already highly price-aware, and fixed-mobile bundles and third-party services can help reduce customer churn.
The spread of eSIM technology has made switching almost frictionless, raising the need for incumbents to adopt AI themselves. Operators can use the technology to improve sales, develop deeper customer insights and target subscribers with personalised upselling or down-selling offers designed to prevent churn.
Pricing gaps indicate where operators face greater exposure. In mobile, entry-level incumbent tariffs in Switzerland, France and Norway are priced 20%, 14% and 11% below second-quarter average revenue per user, respectively, creating greater risk of existing customers moving to cheaper plans.
Competitive pricing pressure is highest in the Netherlands, Switzerland and UK, where challenger offers carry discounts of 71%, 66% and 53% against incumbent back-book pricing. Finland and Italy have much smaller challenger discounts of 7%.
KPN, Swisscom and Virgin Media O2 have the greatest overall mobile exposure based on challenger pricing, spin-down risk and domestic service revenue. Deutsche Telekom, Orange France and Vodafone Germany have more contained exposure.
In fixed broadband, the Netherlands and UK have the highest spin-down risk, with basic incumbent tariffs priced 52% and 51% below second-quarter ARPU. Challenger discounts are greatest in the Netherlands, UK and Italy at 59%, 54% and 50%.
KPN, Virgin Media O2 and Orange France have the highest overall broadband exposure, with Deutsche Telekom, Telia and Telenor better positioned under the pricing analysis.

title: UK PM Burnham to set out economic vision as inflation, Iran war pose challenges
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
Investing.com -- UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham will use next week’s Labour Party conference to outline his economic vision, seeking to project optimism as Britain faces rising inflation, energy costs and the prospect of higher interest rates, Bloomberg reported.
Burnham, who became prime minister after succeeding Keir Starmer in July, is scheduled to deliver the conference keynote Tuesday. His government is also preparing a 10-year plan for December that is expected to provide more detail on its economic programme.
The prime minister has already made reindustrialisation and regional economic development central themes of his government, including establishing a second Downing Street office in Manchester known as No10 North.
The immediate economic environment could complicate those plans. Burnham is preparing to acknowledge that inflation and energy bills may rise over the next six months as the Iran war affects the cost of living.
Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey said Friday that avoiding further interest-rate increases was becoming harder, according to Bloomberg.
Burnham’s government plans to argue that many of the current economic pressures are global and could ease if conditions in the Middle East stabilise. His conference message will centre on restoring confidence in Britain’s economic prospects, with Labour adopting "Hope Again" as its slogan.
The government has already cut VAT on electricity bills and business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues, alongside restoring a £2 cap on bus fares for 2027. Burnham has said the measures were funded through reprioritisation within government spending.
Labour’s longer-term agenda includes shifting more economic authority to UK regions and pursuing closer economic relations with Europe. Burnham has also linked stronger growth to reindustrialisation.
Bloomberg reported that Burnham has received a polling boost since taking office, though Labour remains in a close contest with Reform UK and the Conservatives.
The conference will provide Burnham with an opportunity to add policy detail ahead of the government’s broader 10-year plan expected in December.

title: Germany: Has the fiscal package finally reached the economy?
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
Investing.com -- Germany’s economy appears on course for stronger-than-expected growth in 2026, with early signs that higher government spending is reaching parts of the economy, Citi analysts said.
The fiscal boost is most apparent in defence and government consumption, with infrastructure investment taking longer to feed through into activity.
Defence spending from the core federal budget was 27% higher in the 12 months through August compared with the preceding 12 months. Issuance from Germany’s special fund for defence and investment reached €36.5 billion between January and August, equivalent to 62% of the planned amount for 2026.
Issuance does not necessarily translate immediately into spending, and the transmission has been faster for consumption-related measures. The €6 billion allocated to hospital transformation costs this year is one example, with much of the money effectively transferred to another fund.
Many investment projects remain at relatively early stages. Finance ministry monitoring indicators also show delays across numerous projects, suggesting a larger economic impact from the investment programme may take several more quarters to emerge.
Manufacturing orders provide clearer signs that fiscal support is filtering through. Orders began strengthening about a year ago, following passage of the 2025 budget in September.
The improvement cannot be attributed entirely to government spending. Orders for durable consumer goods, including information technology, communications equipment and other electronics, have increased among both domestic and foreign buyers.
Domestic bulk orders for weapons and ammunition, though, carry a clearer government procurement link. Germany’s domestic manufacturing order backlog has also risen sharply since the 2025 budget was approved.
Infrastructure presents a weaker picture. Civil engineering orders excluding roads have risen 9.3% on a three-month-on-three-month basis, but the series is volatile and does not yet provide firm evidence of accelerating infrastructure investment.
The current data therefore point to an uneven fiscal transmission, with defence procurement and consumption moving faster than large infrastructure projects, whose effects could become more visible in coming quarters.

title: Taiwan says US arms support serves American interests after Trump-Xi summit
full_text:
U.S. stocks post weekly gains, showing resilience despite elevated oil and yields
Investing.com -- Continued U.S. arms sales to Taiwan are in Washington’s national interest by helping the island defend itself and maintain semiconductor production, a senior Taiwanese diplomat said Saturday, Reuters reported.
Taiwan Deputy Foreign Minister Francois Wu made the comments after President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping concluded a three-day summit in Washington without major public breakthroughs on Taiwan and other contentious issues.
Xi told Trump Thursday that he hoped Washington would maintain what Beijing considers the "correct position" of opposing Taiwanese independence.
Wu questioned whether making concessions over Taiwan would serve U.S. interests. He argued that continuing weapons sales and giving Taiwan sufficient defensive capabilities would protect the island from Chinese control and allow its semiconductor industry to keep supplying global markets.
Taiwan is the main producer of advanced chips used in artificial intelligence applications, giving the island a major role in global technology supply chains.
Attention is now focused on a pending U.S. weapons package worth about $14 billion. Trump said after meeting Xi in Beijing in May that the package was being held in abeyance and has not announced a decision following the Washington summit. Reuters previously reported that Beijing wanted Washington to halt arms sales.
The Trump administration approved an $11 billion arms package for Taiwan in December, the largest on record.
Wu said Taipei had maintained continuous communication with Washington surrounding the summit and would continue seeking assurances about U.S. support.
U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue told CNBC Friday that Trump’s Taiwan policy had not changed, including Washington’s position under the Taiwan Relations Act. The law requires the U.S. to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself.
China considers Taiwan part of its territory and has repeatedly opposed U.S. weapons sales to the island. Taiwan’s government rejects Beijing’s sovereignty claims.
China’s People’s Daily reiterated Saturday that Taiwan remains a core Chinese interest and described the issue as a red line in relations with Washington.
